newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai economy powers ahead of China average.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai economy powers ahead of China average.

text.p: Shanghai's economy continues to power ahead of the rest of China with 12.8 percent growth in the first 10 months of the year, according to figures released on Friday.
Analysts said the high growth rate could continue for several years to come with industrial production becoming an increasingly important focus of Shanghai's development.
The Shanghai Statistics Bureau reported that Shanghai's gross domestic product (GDP) for the first 10 months of 1996 was up 12.8 percent over the same 1995 period.
It said the city's GDP in the January-October period was 229.75 billion yuan, while GDP for the month of October was 25.248 billion yuan, up 14.8 percent over October 1995.
Industrial output value for the 10-month period hit 224.76 billion yuan, 18.3 percent up on the corresponding period last year.
Retail sales volume in the January-October period were up 19.8 percent with Shanghai's exports reaching $11.084 billion, an increase of 12.8 percent over the same 1995 period.
Fixed asset investment in the period totalled 103.17 billion yuan this year, a rise of 37.6 percent over the first 10 months of 1995.
China's GDP growth this year has been officially forecast at around 9.6-9.7 percent, compared to 10.5 percent last year.
"The outlook is very bullish in terms of the overall Shanghai economy," said Hoong Yik-luen, head of China research for ING-Barings in Shanghai.
"Shanghai's growth rate will be above the national average for the next four to five years, and also above the rate of the other coastal cities," he added.

"Shanghai aims to build itself into a national centre of finance, information and trade with the central government's support," said Yan Yunlong, deputy general manager of the securities trading department of China Guotai Securities.
"This will help its economy to grow faster than that of the whole nation for the next few years," he added.
Analysts said Shanghai was continuing to pump funds into infrastructure development and basic industry growth which would have a long-term positive effect on the city's growth.

"The structure of investment is changing dramatically with more investment in industry and less in real estate which will have a good effect on employment," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
But he said the figures released Friday, while positive, gave only a partial picture of Shanghai's booming growth.
"There is also the black economy, which is not reflected in these numbers at all," he said. "I think it's huge, but no one, not even the government, knows how big it is."

He said the obvious improvements to dress and lifestyle amongst Shanghai people over the past year or so, at a time when the state economy was supposed to be emerging slowly from a recession, was an indication of the power of the black economy.
